chicha.name: Chicha
chicha.summary: A traditional Andean and Amazonian beverage, most commonly a corn beer called chicha de jora, used ceremonially in the Inca Empire.

chenopodium-pallidicaule.name: Cañihua
chenopodium-pallidicaule.summary: An Andean relative of quinoa, with over 200 varieties, farmed in the Altiplano for millennia and valued for its high protein, fiber and phenolic content.

ullucus.name: Ulluco
ullucus.summary: A root vegetable grown in the Andes since Inca times, second only to the potato in importance as an Andean tuber crop, with brightly coloured waxy skin.

arracacia-xanthorrhiza.name: Arracacha
arracacia-xanthorrhiza.summary: A starchy root vegetable native to the Andes, grown as a major food crop across South America.

lupinus-mutabilis.name: Tarwi
lupinus-mutabilis.summary: An Andean lupin species grown mainly for its protein-rich, oil-yielding bean, whose natural bitterness comes from alkaloids that must be removed before eating.

canna-indica.name: Achira (Canna indica)
canna-indica.summary: A plant native to the Americas, also called Indian shot or edible canna, grown for its starchy, edible rhizomes.

cusco.name: Cusco
cusco.summary: City in southeastern Peru founded in the 12th century as capital of the Kingdom of Cusco and later the Inca Empire; today a UNESCO World Heritage site and major tourist destination.

tiwanaku.name: Tiwanaku
tiwanaku.summary: A major pre-Columbian archaeological site in Bolivia near Lake Titicaca, home to an estimated 10,000 to 20,000 people around 800 CE, with monumental structures and megalithic stonework.

chimor.name: Chimor
chimor.summary: A pre-Inca kingdom of the Chimú culture on Peru's coast, arising about 900 CE and conquered by the Inca around 1470; Guacricur, grandson of its founder Taycanamo, expanded its rule over the lower valley.

chan-chan.name: Chan Chan
chan-chan.summary: Capital city of the Chimor kingdom in northern Peru, and the largest city of pre-Columbian South America, built from about 900 CE until conquered by the Inca in 1470.

sacsayhuam-n.name: Sacsayhuamán
sacsayhuam-n.summary: An Inca citadel near Cusco, Peru, built with massive interlocking stone walls, traditionally said to date from the reign of Pachacuti and his successors; now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

metropolitan-cathedral-of-lima.name: Metropolitan Cathedral of Lima
metropolitan-cathedral-of-lima.summary: The main Roman Catholic cathedral of Lima, Peru, begun by Francisco Pizarro in 1535 and completed in 1797; it is the oldest and largest church in the country.

ovalle.name: Ovalle
ovalle.summary: A Chilean city founded in 1831 in the Coquimbo Region, named after former vice president José Tomás Ovalle, set amid a mining district.

chanka.name: Chanka
chanka.summary: An Andean ethnic group and chiefdom that fought the Incas and, according to colonial-era accounts, once besieged Cusco before being defeated in the Inca-Chanka wars.

viracocha-inca.name: Viracocha Inca
viracocha-inca.summary: Eighth Sapa Inka of the Kingdom of Cuzco, ruling from around 1410 to 1438 as the third ruler of the Hanan dynasty.

qullasuyu.name: Qullasuyu
qullasuyu.summary: The largest of the four quarters of the Inca Empire, covering the Bolivian Altiplano and much of the southern Andes into northwest Argentina and Chile.

topa-inca-yupanqui.name: Topa Inca Yupanqui
topa-inca-yupanqui.summary: Tenth Sapa Inca of the Inca Empire, reigning from 1471 to 1493, son of Pachacuti and father of Huayna Capac.

battle-of-the-maule.name: Battle of the Maule
battle-of-the-maule.summary: A battle, traditionally dated to the late 1400s, in which Mapuche forces halted the Inca Empire's southward expansion near Chile's Maule River, though its date and importance are disputed.

mapuche.name: Mapuche
mapuche.summary: An Indigenous people of south-central Chile and southwestern Argentina, with a traditional economy based on agriculture and material culture known for textiles and silverwork.

maule-river.name: Maule River
maule-river.summary: A major Chilean river tied to the country's Inca-era, colonial and independence history, which marked the Inca Empire's southern frontier.

chachapoya-culture.name: Chachapoya
chachapoya-culture.summary: An Andean people called the 'Warriors of the Clouds' who lived in Peru's cloud forests, resisting Inca conquest before being absorbed into the Inca Empire shortly before the Spanish arrived.

mitma.name: Mitma
mitma.summary: An Inca policy of forcibly resettling whole communities to newly conquered lands to spread loyalty and Inca culture, affecting roughly a quarter to a third of the empire's population.

ku-lap.name: Kuélap
ku-lap.summary: A walled settlement in the mountains of the Amazonas region of Peru, built by the Chachapoyas culture in the 6th century AD overlooking the Utcubamba Valley.

pachacuti.name: Pachacuti
pachacuti.summary: Ninth Sapa Inca of Cusco, who transformed it into the Inca Empire through conquest and is believed to have had Machu Picchu built as a royal estate.

canta-district.name: Canta
canta-district.summary: One of seven districts of Peru's Canta province.

wari-culture.name: Wari culture
wari-culture.summary: A Middle Horizon civilization flourishing across the south-central Andes and coastal Peru from about 500 to 1000 AD, which at its height formed the Wari Empire centered near modern Ayacucho.

coricancha.name: Coricancha
coricancha.summary: The most important temple of the Inca Empire, located in Cusco, Peru; its name means "golden temple" in Quechua.

quitu-culture.name: Quitu
quitu-culture.summary: A pre-Columbian Indigenous people of Ecuador who founded Quito and ruled the area from around 2000 BCE until overtaken by the Inca; they built elaborate deep tombs around 800 CE.

quipu.name: Quipu
quipu.summary: Knotted-cord record-keeping devices used by Andean cultures, especially the Inca, to store numbers and other data in a decimal positional system; they date back to at least the 1st millennium CE.

moche-valley.name: Moche Valley
moche-valley.summary: A fertile valley in northern Peru around the Moche River, farmed since pre-Columbian times and now home to the city of Trujillo.

quechuan-languages.name: Quechua language
quechuan-languages.summary: Indigenous language family that originated in central Peru and spread through the Andes, the most widely spoken pre-Columbian language family in the Americas and the primary language of the Inca Empire.

aymara-language.name: Aymara language
aymara-language.summary: An indigenous language of the Bolivian Andes with over a million speakers, an official language of Bolivia and Peru alongside Spanish and Quechua.

ollantay.name: Ollantay
ollantay.summary: A Quechua-language play, possibly of Inca origin, considered among the oldest expressions of Quechua literature; its oldest manuscript dates from the 18th century.

moray-inca-ruin.name: Moray
moray-inca-ruin.summary: An Inca archaeological site in Peru with terraced circular depressions up to 30 meters deep, whose design creates a temperature difference of up to 15°C between top and bottom.

tip-n.name: Tipón
tip-n.summary: An early 15th-century Inca archaeological site near Cusco, Peru, famous for its advanced irrigation terraces and canal system.

chasqui.name: Chasqui
chasqui.summary: A trained running messenger of the Inca Empire who relayed messages and small packages along the road system, covering up to 300 kilometres a day via relay stations.

quechua-people.name: Quechua people
quechua-people.summary: Indigenous peoples of South America, native mainly to Peru, who speak Quechuan languages; the Incas of Cusco began as one such group before expanding.

urcos.name: Urcos
urcos.summary: A small town in eastern Peru where, by tradition, an Inca ruler received visions of the creator god Viracocha and took the name Viracocha Inca.

sapa-inca.name: Sapa Inca
sapa-inca.summary: The Quechua title for the Inca Empire's supreme monarch, believed to be the sun god's son, a hereditary position held from around 1100 CE until Atahualpa's execution in 1533.

kingdom-of-cusco.name: Kingdom of Cusco
kingdom-of-cusco.summary: A small Andean city-state founded by the Incas around the start of the 13th century that grew, through conquest and alliance, into the Inca Empire by 1438.

ayacucho.name: Ayacucho
ayacucho.summary: A city in the Peruvian Andes, originally called Huamanga until 1825, when Simón Bolívar renamed it to honor the battle that secured Peru's independence.

antisuyu.name: Antisuyu
antisuyu.summary: The eastern quarter of the Inca Empire, bordering the Upper Amazon region, inhabited by the varied ethnic groups collectively called Antis.

ayllu.name: Ayllu
ayllu.summary: A traditional Andean kinship-based community with its own territory, functioning to organize farming and social life before, during and after Inca rule.

taulichusco.name: Taulichusco
taulichusco.summary: An Incan kuraka who governed part of the Rímac Valley in the mid-16th century; a monument in Lima still commemorates him.

huayna-capac.name: Huayna Capac
huayna-capac.summary: Eleventh Sapa Inca of the Inca Empire, ruling from before 1493 until his death in 1527, under whom Tawantinsuyu reached its greatest territorial extent. His death sparked the Inca Civil War between his sons Huáscar and Atahualpa.

government-palace-peru.name: Government Palace, Peru
government-palace-peru.summary: The seat of Peru's executive branch and official presidential residence in Lima, first built by Francisco Pizarro in 1535 on the site of an earlier indigenous shrine.

mar-a-rostworowski.name: María Rostworowski
mar-a-rostworowski.summary: Peruvian historian (1915–2016) known for extensive, detailed publications on ancient Peruvian cultures and the Inca Empire.

huaca.name: Huaca
huaca.summary: In Quechuan languages, an object or place considered sacred, often a monument or natural feature believed to hold spirits.

viracocha.name: Viracocha
viracocha.summary: Creator and supreme deity of pre-Inca and Inca mythology, said to have made the universe, sun, moon, stars and time, and to have ordered the building of Tiwanaku.

inti.name: Inti
inti.summary: The ancient Inca sun god, revered as national patron of the Inca state and believed to have been born of the creator deity Viracocha.

chav-n-culture.name: Chavín culture
chav-n-culture.summary: A pre-Columbian civilization in Peru's northern Andean highlands, flourishing roughly 900 to 250 BCE, marked by an intensified religious cult and advances in ceramics, agriculture, metallurgy and textiles.

nazca-culture.name: Nazca culture
nazca-culture.summary: An archaeological culture that flourished from about 100 BC to 800 AD on Peru's southern coast, known for ceramics, textiles, geoglyphs, and underground aqueducts called puquios.

huanchaco.name: Huanchaco
huanchaco.summary: A seaside resort city near Trujillo, Peru, known for surfing and reed fishing boats, close to the ancient ruins of Chan Chan.

manco-c-pac.name: Manco Cápac
manco-c-pac.summary: Traditionally regarded as the first ruler and founder of the Inca civilization at Cusco, possibly in the early 13th century, and a central figure in Inca origin myths, though his actual existence remains uncertain.

mama-ocllo.name: Mama Ocllo
mama-ocllo.summary: Inca mythological mother and fertility goddess said to have founded Cusco with her brother-husband Manco Cápac and taught Inca women spinning and household skills.

ceque-system.name: Ceque system
ceque-system.summary: A network of 41 or 42 ritual pathways radiating from Cusco's sun temple across the Inca Empire's four regions, linking sacred shrines called huacas.

reiner-tom-zuidema.name: R. Tom Zuidema
reiner-tom-zuidema.summary: An anthropologist (1927–2016), professor at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, known for his structural analysis of Inca social organization, including the ceque system and Inca calendar.

chiribaya-culture.name: Chiribaya culture
chiribaya-culture.summary: A culture that flourished along the coast of southern Peru and Chile from 700 CE until Spanish colonization, combining coastal fishing settlements with inland farming communities, notably studied in the Osmore valley.

ilo-peru.name: Ilo
ilo-peru.summary: A port city in southern Peru with about 69,376 people, the second largest city in the Moquegua Region and capital of Ilo Province.

humboldt-current.name: Humboldt Current
humboldt-current.summary: A cold ocean current flowing north along South America's Pacific coast, named after Alexander von Humboldt though discovered earlier by José de Acosta; its upwelling supports rich marine life and about a fifth of the world's fish catch.

trujillo-peru.name: Trujillo, Peru
trujillo-peru.summary: A city on Peru's northwestern coast, site of the earlier Moche and Chimú cultures, later declared the provisional capital of Peru by Bolívar in 1824.

lima.name: Limaq
lima.summary: The native Quechua name for the region where the Peruvian capital Lima was later founded, giving the city its modern name.

r-mac-river.name: Rímac Valley
r-mac-river.summary: The valley in western Peru through which the Rímac River flows, home to the city of Lima and several smaller towns between the coast and mountains.

osmore-river.name: Osmore River
osmore-river.summary: A river system in southern coastal Peru, rising in the Andes and known by different names along its course, whose valley holds archaeological sites spanning 10,000 years.

pedro-cieza-de-le-n.name: Pedro Cieza de León
pedro-cieza-de-le-n.summary: Spanish conquistador and chronicler (c. 1518–1554) whose Crónicas del Perú is considered fundamental to understanding Inca history and the empire's structure.

azapa-valley.name: Azapa Valley
azapa-valley.summary: A fertile oasis valley near Arica, Chile, known for its unusual climate and distinctive violet-colored olives.

chinchorro-culture.name: Chinchorro culture
chinchorro-culture.summary: A preceramic fishing culture on the coast of what is now northern Chile and southern Peru, lasting from about 7,000 to 1,500 BCE and famous for elaborate mummification; named a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2021.
